title: Payment System
summary: Design a payment platform that charges customers, pays merchants, and stays correct under failures.
statement: Design a payment system used by online merchants. It accepts payment requests, talks to external payment providers, records every movement in a ledger, supports refunds, and must never lose or duplicate a charge. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Record every movement in a ledger.

requirementQuestions.question: Can a customer ever be charged twice or not at all, and how are such cases resolved?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Selects between strong and eventual models and shapes conflict handling.

requirementQuestions.question: How many transactions per second, and how spiky?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: What if a provider is slow or down?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: How is card data handled and which compliance rules apply?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Introduces authentication, authorisation, and privacy constraints that affect the design.

requirementQuestions.question: How long are records kept and how are they audited?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

requirementQuestions.question: Which payment methods, currencies, and refund flows are supported?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How many ledger entries per day?
How much capacity is needed for peak sales?
What fraction of requests need provider retries?

keyDecisions.question: How are duplicates prevented?
considerations: Client-supplied idempotency keys stored with results.
Handling a timeout whose outcome is unknown.

keyDecisions.question: How is progress tracked?
considerations: Explicit states persisted before and after each provider call.

keyDecisions.question: How are money movements recorded?
considerations: Double-entry bookkeeping in an append-only ledger.

keyDecisions.question: How are external providers used?
considerations: Adapters per provider with circuit breakers.

keyDecisions.question: How is correctness verified?
considerations: Compare internal records with provider reports daily.

tradeoffs.tension: Simple UX versus resilience to slow providers.
Money requires correctness; some operations may be delayed.

commonMistakes: Retrying a provider call without idempotency.
Storing only balances and no ledger.
followUps: How do you handle partial refunds?
How do you design for PCI compliance?
How do you add a new payment method?
